attributes.comment:
The proposed framework appropriately focuses on decision quality, efficiency, and safety monitoring in early-phase clinical trials.

However, there is a critical evaluation dimension that is not currently addressed:

whether an AI-supported recommendation is admissible at the moment it is acted upon.

Early-phase trials are characterized by high uncertainty, evolving patient state, and incomplete information. Under these conditions, even high-quality or statistically valid recommendations may become misaligned with the current clinical or trial context by the time they are executed.

Current evaluation categories assess:

how accurate or useful a recommendation is
how efficiently decisions are made
how safety signals are detected

But they do not assess:

whether there is sufficient state, authority, and evidence to justify acting on that recommendation at the point of execution

This creates a structural gap:

A system may generate a high-quality recommendation that is:

contextually outdated
based on incomplete or shifting patient data
no longer aligned with trial conditions

…and still influence a clinical or regulatory action without a mechanism to prevent execution under insufficient conditions.

To address this, the pilot program should include an additional evaluation dimension:

Execution Admissibility

Systems should be evaluated on their ability to:

determine whether sufficient state, authority, and evidence are present at the moment of action
prevent or delay execution when those conditions are not met
provide a traceable record of why an action was allowed, held, or denied

This shifts evaluation from:

decision quality alone

to:

decision + justified execution under real-world conditions

Without this layer, improvements in AI-driven decision-making may increase the speed and volume of actions taken, without ensuring those actions remain justified at the time they occur.

In early-phase trials, where uncertainty is highest, this distinction is critical to maintaining patient safety, trial integrity, and regulatory defensibility.
